title: HTTP request and response lifecycle
description: Trace an HTTP request from the moment the user hits enter through the network, server processing, and response delivery.

data.text: After DNS, TCP, and TLS are complete, the browser is finally ready to speak HTTP. The request lifecycle covers parsing the URL, sending headers and body, waiting for the server, receiving the response, and handing data to the renderer. Each stage is a place where delays, errors, or misconfigurations can appear.

data.title: Lifecycle stages
items: User enters URL or clicks a link.
Browser parses the URL into protocol, host, port, and path.
If needed, a redirect is followed before any network call.
Browser checks HTTP cache for a fresh copy.
If cache misses, TCP/TLS handshakes happen.
Browser constructs the request line, headers, and optional body.
Request bytes travel over the network to the server.
Server routes the request, runs application logic, and queries databases if needed.
Server builds a response with status line, headers, and optional body.
Response bytes travel back to the browser.
Browser processes the response: decodes, caches, and parses.
The renderer displays the page or executes JavaScript.

data.caption: High-level HTTP request and response lifecycle
data.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A[User action] --> B[Parse URL]
    B --> C{Cache hit?}
    C -->|yes| D[Return cached response]
    C -->|no| E[TCP/TLS handshake]
    E --> F[Send request]
    F --> G[Server processing]
    G --> H[Send response]
    H --> I[Browser decode]
    I --> J[Render page]

data.title: What you can measure
data.text: Browser DevTools Network tab exposes almost every stage: DNS time, TCP/TLS time, TTFB, content download, and total time. Use these columns to localize slowness.

An HTTP request consists of a request line, headers, and optionally a body. The request line contains the method, path, and HTTP version. Headers carry metadata like cookies, content type, and authorization.

data.title: Minimal HTTP request
data.content: A typical GET request looks like this:
data.code:
GET /blog/first-post HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0
Accept: text/html
Cookie: session=abc123

data.text: The response starts with a status line containing the HTTP version, status code, and reason phrase. Headers follow, then a blank line, then the optional body.

data.title: Typical HTTP response
data.content: A successful response might look like:
data.code:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 4821
Cache-Control: max-age=3600

<!doctype html><html>...

data.title: Common latency sources
items: Slow DNS resolution or DNS propagation delays
TCP/TLS handshake overhead on high-latency networks
Server-side processing time, often database queries
Large response bodies over slow connections
Browser rendering blocked by synchronous JavaScript

data.title: Server processing is usually the bottleneck
data.text: Network latency is rarely the dominant cost. If your backend takes 400 ms to build a response, optimizing TLS or TCP will not fix the user experience.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: The HTTP lifecycle spans URL parsing, caching, networking, server processing, and rendering.
Request and response messages both have a structured start-line, headers, and optional body.
Browser DevTools can isolate delays to specific stages.
Server-side processing is the most common performance bottleneck.
data.takeaway: Tracing the full request lifecycle helps you know which layer to optimize when a page feels slow.

items.question: What is TTFB?
items.answer: Time To First Byte is the interval between sending the request and receiving the first byte of the response. It includes network latency and server processing time.

items.question: Why does the browser sometimes show '(pending)'?
items.answer: The request is queued because the browser limits concurrent connections per origin. The queue is normal; it prevents overwhelming the server or saturating the network.

items.question: Does the body always come after headers?
items.answer: In HTTP/1.x and HTTP/2, yes. HTTP/3 uses QUIC streams but still frames headers and body separately.

data.text: You cannot optimize what you cannot measure. The Network panel is your primary diagnostic tool for request lifecycle issues.
